newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Enron CEO sees boom in Europe gas market.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Enron CEO sees boom in Europe gas market.

text.p: Europe's competitive natural gas market is set for phenomenal growth and will be worth $250 billion by the end of the next decade, the Chairman and CEO of United States gas giant Enron Corp Kenneth Lay told Reuters on Monday.
"Within the next five years there will be a $100 billion retail market in Europe and by the middle or end of next decade the retail and wholesale markets will be worth $250 billion," Lay said.
This would echo the huge growth in the United States where the combined markets for natural gas and electricity continue to see liberalisation at the retail level.
"The combined retail market for electricity and natural gas will be worth $3 billion (in the U.S.) this year," said Lay.
"In 1998, this will be $30 billion. And by 2001 a $150 billion market will be wide open for competition - that's two thirds to three quarters of all retail natural gas and electricity business."
Including the wholesale sector, Lay puts the total size of the electricity and natural gas market in the U.S. at $300 billion.
Lay said he was encouraged by the progress made opening up the energy market in parts of Europe other than Britain. He saw the European Commission talking of phasing in deregulation over nine years.
"We're in favour of a more accelerated schedule," he added, seeing liberalisation as inevitable. "It's hard to imagine how any one country can hold out."
"Germany will probably be first," Lay continued, but added that progress has also been made in the Netherlands.
"It's irresistible in that it results in much lower energy costs," he said. "I've yet to see any market where competition led to higher prices."
Enron is already active across Europe.
It supplies up to four percent of Britain's electricity through its Teesside power station in the North East of England, and in March will start work on a further plant in Lincolnshire, east England.
Enron also has stakes in plants in former East Germany and Sardinia, and a planned plant in Turkey.
But the company has also been dogged by a legal dispute over North Sea gas supply.
Enron has contracted to buy gas under a long-term contract from the J-Block area, owned by producer Phillips Petroleum, Agip and British Gas Exploration and Production Ltd.

But it told them that it would not take delivery of gas until late 1998 because of a slump in British gas prices, and refused a Commissioning Date, so seeking to defer the start of its obligations to pay for the contracted gas.
The two sides are currently involved in litigation.
"The best way to characterise J-Block is difficult," said Lay. Enron would continue to diversify its sources, he added.

"We're sourcing gas from all over Europe. We're looking to other markets, other projects, we have a long term relationship with (Russian gas monopoly) Gazprom, we buy gas from other sources in the North Sea," Lay said.
Enron's share of the U.S. markets for both gas and electricity continues to grow.
Last year the company sold around eight billion British Thermal Units (btu) a day of gas, accounting for some 16 or 17 percent of the market there and, Lay believes, the largest market share.
This year Enron is on course to extend this to nine billion btu.

In 1990, he said, Enron had eight percent of the market, the next nine largest suppliers had 40 percent, and others had 52 percent. Now Enron has 16 percent, the next nine largest have 76 percent and the others are down to a mere eight percent.
"It's become more consolidated and rationalised", Lay said.
In electricity, Enron made its first physical sales in early 1994. By the first quarter of this year, it has sales of 33 million MW hours, he said.
"I believe we are now the largest independent non-utility marketer in the U.S., but also the largest overall wholesale marketer," he said.
One of Enron's biggest competitors in the U.S. is American Electric Power Co Inc, which announced on Monday it was to acquire Britain's Yorkshire Electricity Group plc.
Lay would not be drawn on the acquisition, other than to say "the main question is one of timing. If there's a change of government, the matter will be taken up by the new government."
Asked about Enron's view of a possible change of government in Britain, Lay appeared sanguine.
"Like everybody else we're trying to get acquainted with shadow ministers, as well as working closely with government ministers," he said.
